extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humour studies, social psychology, cultural studies, and literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for analysing and judging jokes with respect to their form, content, target, context, ethics, and social effects — especially the distinction between 'joke-work' (technique) and tendentious/purposive content. Useful for academic critique or teaching on humour theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form versus content (joke-work vs tendentious purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: What counts in producing large amounts of laughter is the underlying content and not the joke-form; the same joke-work can produce different reactions depending on the tendentious content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud's observation: if both tendentious and innocent jokes use similar technical devices, greater laughter of tendentious jokes must come from sources of pleasure available to tendentious jokes alone. Examples: the 'home-roulard' pun can be innocent formally but function tendentiously in context; the tiling joke has racist and feminist variants that share identical joke-work but differ radically in reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standard joke techniques (condensation, displacement, double meanings, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical mechanisms such as condensation, displacement, and double meanings are common features of jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both innocent and tendentious jokes employ these devices; therefore technical cleverness alone does not explain why some jokes provoke more or less laughter. Freud notes joke techniques may be 'quite wretched' yet provoke laughter—so catalogue technique but do not treat it as decisive for ethical or impact judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendentiousness / ulterior purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a joke has a purposive, often aggressive or sexual, intent beyond mere wordplay (a tendentious purpose) — such purposes provide sources of pleasure not available to innocent jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud: 'Only jokes that have a purpose run the risk of meeting with people who do not want to listen to them.' Identify aggressive, hostile, sexual, or political aims hidden behind apparent wit; these aims explain both intense laughter and potential disapproval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of target
rubrics_metrics.description: The target chosen by a joke strongly affects recipients' reactions; social position and identity of the target matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings: subordinates prefer jokes that mock superiors and vice versa (Zillman 1983). Ethnic, gender, or status-based targets change enjoyment markedly (examples: Jewish/Arab targets in Israel; Danish/Norwegian jokes). When evaluating a joke, record who is targeted and how audience positionality will shape responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taboo and aggressive content increases enjoyment (but varies individually)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes about taboo topics (sex, aggression) are often enjoyed more than jokes about non-taboo topics, though preferences vary between individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Kuhlman (1985) and Herzog/Bush (1994): taboo topics often provoke stronger amusement. When assessing a joke's effect, note its taboo content and expect variability across audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and audience like-mindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The same joke can be enjoyed differently depending on the immediate conversational context and whether the audience is like-minded (insiders) or likely to interpret it as hostile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pun at an awkward conversational moment can function as put-down; sexually tendentious jokes told within same-sex groups are more acceptable. Always evaluate context of telling (setting, timing, relationships) alongside content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insider versus outsider status of teller
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the teller belongs to the group that is the butt of the joke affects classification and acceptability; insider jokes often incorporate self-recognition while outsider jokes can be mere derision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud's distinction for Jewish jokes: jokes told by Jews differ from those told by non-Jews. Insiders may 'acknowledge their real faults as well as the connection between them and their good qualities' whereas outsider jokes can be 'brutal derision.' Note teller identity when judging harm or legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral appropriateness and risk of disapproval ('unlaughter')
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke liable to intense laughter in one context can evoke strong moral disapproval in another; assess potential for 'unlaughter' where audience judges the target morally inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud links tendentious humour with moral judgement: pleasure and disapproval are two possible responses. When critiquing, consider moral standards of relevant audiences and the likelihood of backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients’ misattribution / self-deception about why they laugh
rubrics_metrics.description: People often believe they laugh because of clever joke-work rather than because of tendentious content; they are 'poor judges' of what makes them laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud and Zillman: subjects attribute amusement to joke technique not target. Analysts should probe beyond self-reports of amusement to identify whether content (targeting, aggression, taboo) is the real cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teasing as social control and rhetorical deflection ('tease-spray')
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling behaviour as 'teasing' or 'just a joke' can function to control recipients and deflect criticism, protecting jokers from accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical work (Keltner et al.; Hepburn) shows teasers overestimate recipients' enjoyment and use 'teasing' rhetoric to avoid self-criticism. When evaluating humour, distinguish genuine playful teasing with consent from rhetorical 'tease-spray' used to immunize mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact-over-intent evaluation (effects matter more than jokers' claimed beliefs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke's social effect—whether it recycles stereotypes or validates prejudice—should be central to evaluation rather than whether the joker claims not to believe the stereotype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debates: Davies defends ethnic jokes as harmless because jokers may not believe stereotypes; critics emphasize that laughter still validates prejudiced images. Focus critique on consequences and reinforcement of stereotypes, not solely declared intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'pure aggression' violent jokes from stereotype-based jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Pure aggression' jokes play explicitly with violence as the source of humour, while many ethnic jokes rely on stereotyped attributes; both have different ethical and social implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'three blacks at the bottom of a river' is 'pure violent' humour found on KKK sites; lawyer versions are unreal and hyperbolic, racist versions treat actual violence as fun. Identify whether violence is fantasized or endorses real-world harm when assessing offensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and framing affect acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: The source and framing of a joke (e.g., cited provenance, presentation context) can make it more or less acceptable to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud cited an artists' carnival as provenance for the umbrella joke to reassure readers. When analyzing or presenting controversial jokes, note framing devices that might be used to legitimize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and omission bias in theoretical examples
rubrics_metrics.description: What theorists include or omit (e.g., Freud's near-absence of sexual or racist jokes) influences theoretical claims about humour; omissions can be theoretically significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically assess whether the corpus used to support a theory is skewed by an author’s choices. Freud's omissions shape his portrayal of humour as rebellious; account for such selection effects when drawing generalisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical cleverness is not a sufficient defence for offensive humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguing a joke is 'technically better' (funnier) does not negate its offensiveness; offensive humour should not be excused merely because it is witty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cautions anti-racists not to object on grounds of technical quality alone. When evaluating, separate craft (wit, cleverness) from ethical evaluation (racist, sexist content) — both matter but are distinct issues.
